articles.title_orig: Traffic Control Errors Caused Spain’s Deadly Train Crash, Official Says
articles.title_zh: Traffic Control Errors Caused Spain’s Deadly Train Crash, Official Says
articles.content_orig:
The breaking news from Spain this week was shocking but also shockingly familiar: another collision on the high-speed rail line south from Madrid, with reports of dozens killed.
It is just nine months since two trains crashed near Cordoba, killing 46 people. Now 69 bodies have been recovered here in central Spain, from wreckage strewn over the tracks and down an embankment.
For the victims' families it is devastating; a personal tragedy.
But it is also a national disaster that has shattered confidence in the country's rail network and the Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez. It is playing out just weeks before the snap general election he called.
The formal investigation into the Toledo train disaster has only just been launched but the government has been quick to take control of the narrative.
From the first hours after the collision, Transport Minister Oscar Puente began suggesting "human error" was to blame, batting responsibility as far as possible from the cabinet.
On Friday, he appeared before the press for a second time to set out what he called the "objective facts" of the crash and counter a surge of criticism against the government.
The opposition People's Party (PP) is among those calling for his resignation as a "moral" and "ethical" move.
Instead after expressing "huge pain and sadness" for the victims, Puente went on the offensive.
He rejected talk of chronic underinvestment in infrastructure and insisted that Spain's high-speed signalling safety system, the LZB, was neither old nor inadequate: Germany and Austria use the same.
In Spain, it has already failed 170 times so far this year, he revealed, but called that "normal" and around the EU average.
The problem surrounds what happens next - when the system fails and control of the line shifts to manual.
In this case, the minister highlighted a series of human errors that proved catastrophic.
Crucially, at one point a controller instructed a stalled train to restart, clearing it to advance at up to 160km/h (100 mph) even though a second train was stuck on the line up ahead.
The impending collision was clear from audio calls and on big screens in the control centre in Madrid.
"They worked. We checked. They could see what was happening," Puente confirmed. But the advancing train was never ordered to stop.
"I'm no judge... But these are the facts."
So would he take personal and political responsibility anyway, and resign? Puente called it his "duty", rather, to remain as minister.
"I'll face up to things, explain, elucidate," he countered. "I'll think how to improve the system, and give confidence to those who want to travel by train and feel calm and safe."
But Spaniards will take a lot of persuading.
"This is not only a very serious accident, but the second in a very short time," Paco Camas of the pollster Ipsos points out.
An investigation into January's crash in Adamuz , near Cordoba, is still open, with initial reports suggesting there was a crack in the rails -  very different to the latest collision.
But there is a similar impact.
"It destroys people's confidence not only in the railways but institutions in general," Camas warns. "And in Spain when such things happen, we know that people blame their government."
For Team Sánchez it is the latest in a spiral of crises.
Allegations of corruption against the prime minister's close relatives still persist, all denied.
Then there was a sudden influx of migrants from Morocco this summer to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. That got right-wing opponents shouting about incompetence and underfunding.
Later, a video of a pensioner being forcibly evicted from her home went viral and sparked street protests.
That's when Sánchez called an early election .
His chances of winning the vote looked slim even before the train crash. Now they have plummeted.
Most recent polls showed the centre-right PP coming first and forming a coalition with the far-right Vox.
"They have this majority in almost 95% of the simulations we have done," Prof Pablo Simon of Madrid's Carlos III University explains.
But Sánchez had been running a positive campaign, trying to lure apathetic voters to the polls to vote socialist.
Suddenly, the tone has changed.
"They've totally lost control of the agenda and the emotion of this campaign," Simon says. "It's going to be extremely difficult now. There is this general mood of decay, of a country that's not working properly. A depression."
There have already been small protests over the train crash led by far-right groups in Madrid and large numbers of police are on stand-by this weekend ahead of further potential clashes, organised online.
Here in Toledo, the mood is nervous.
"We all travelled in silence and really sad," Paloma told me at the city station, where she had just pulled in on a half empty train.
She admitted she's scared of the high-speed network now and angry at the government.
"This crash will change all of our votes, completely," Paloma said. "We'll shift from the left wing to the right. Because of everything that's happened."
Lucia takes the high-speed AVE into Madrid each day, and is scared too.
"This was human error. But there's been two accidents now with more than 100 dead," she says. "Things here are really bad. They have to change."
Producer Davide Ghiglione contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
articles.title_zh: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
articles.content_orig:
Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.
The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.
One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.
This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.
On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.
This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.
"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."
The past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.
Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".
Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."
In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions.
"If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."
From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son.
"Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children," one of his letters reads, "The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom."
Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.
Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.
But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.
The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.
That changed on 3 August 2020.
That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.
In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.
In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.
At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.
But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.
One of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.
She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.
A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame.
She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy.
"I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve.
"I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."
In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté.
"It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."
Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.

articles.title_orig: Meta’s Rating Outlook Cut to Negative by S&P on AI Spending
articles.title_zh: Meta’s Rating Outlook Cut to Negative by S&P on AI Spending
articles.content_orig:
Meta's outlook has been revised downward by S&P Global Ratings on concerns surrounding cash flow and AI spending.
The credit agency said Friday that the outlook reflects "uncertainty" about Meta's elevated capex and its negative free cash flow.
Meta's credit rating was revised from AA- stable to AA- negative, S&P said. S&Ps highest credit rating is AAA. Anything below BBB falls into the junk bond category.
The agency questioned "Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments" relative to its peers, which are also spending heavily on data center buildouts and going cash flow negative in the process.
Although Meta has recently debuted its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models, S&P said "it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years."
A Meta spokesperson pushed back on the revision.
"We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," the spokesperson said in a statement. "We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile."
Meta said in its third-quarter earnings report last week that it expects full-year capex to come in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, going in the red for the first time.
Investors sent Meta shares down 7% following the report despite a revenue beat. The stock finished October down 15%, its worst month in four years.
The company said on Monday that it plans to raise $95 billion to help fund its AI initiatives, with plans to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, followed by an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program.
S&P said that while it expects Meta's capex growth to start "flattening out beginning in 2028," the agency is "less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated."

articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Hedge Fund Arini Offloads $800 Million in Debt as Losses Deepen
articles.content_orig:
Arini losses deepen to 26% as European junk bond selloff accelerates
October 29, 2026 at 9:43 am
Arini Capital Management's flagship hedge fund has lost approximately 26% this year as a selloff in Europe's riskiest corporate debt forces the $21.7bn credit manager to adopt a more defensive investment approach, according to a report by Bloomberg.
The fund, which managed $7.5bn at the end of July, is on course for its first annual loss since founder Hamza Lemssouguer launched the strategy in 2022. Lemssouguer, a former Credit Suisse credit trader, has reportedly reduced new purchases to focus on managing existing positions, withdrawing a significant source of liquidity from Europe's distressed debt market.
The retreat comes as European triple-C rated corporate bonds face their longest losing streak since 2018, with October potentially marking their worst monthly performance in four years. Rising interest rates, higher energy prices and concerns over corporate creditworthiness have intensified pressure on heavily indebted borrowers, while other credit hedge funds have also suffered losses. Sona Asset Management's flagship fund declined 3.1% in the first half of October, putting it on course for its worst month since launching in 2016.
Arini's concentrated exposure to distressed borrowers has contributed to the drawdown, including positions in Aston Martin and Altice International. Aston Martin's bonds fell from approximately 55 cents on the dollar at the beginning of October to 47 cents by Wednesday, while debt issued by Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection has dropped below 75 cents from more than 92 cents at the end of September. Some investors have reportedly become reluctant to purchase securities in which Arini holds sizeable positions.
Despite the losses, Arini continues to attract capital, having raised $1.5bn for its credit strategy and reopened the fund to existing investors. More than $400m of the new commitments was allocated at the beginning of October, with the remainder scheduled for deployment through February.
The downturn marks a sharp reversal for a manager whose flagship fund returned 25.8% in 2023, 20.8% in 2024 and 8.6% in 2025. However, some credit investors believe the market dislocation could create opportunities to acquire distressed securities at attractive valuations, even as concerns grow over further losses across Europe's lowest-rated debt markets.

articles.title_orig: Village in the Shade Review
articles.title_zh: Village in the Shade Review
articles.content_orig:
It would have been easy for Village in the Shade to just be another farming sim, but with a twist. The genre is a dime a dozen these days, and while not every dog has had its day - it's hard not to feel that Square Enix may have tipped their hats just a bit too early with Harvestella, for instance - it's clear that there's an insatiable desire from players to envision a cozy farming life. Carefree, beyond the simple need to tend your crops and feed your animals; not a real worry in sight.
In typical NIS fashion, Village in the Shade is decidedly not that type of farming game. While there is a "Village in the Sunshine" mode that turns it into one, this is a trap; what makes Village in the Shade special are the moments where the game looks directly at the player and asks you what drives you to pursue a peaceful farming life, and exactly what sort of friction you'd be willing to deal with in the name of that peaceful existence.
That's not to say that the game slacks on its farming sim chops, or just uses it as set dressing for the nuanced story it's trying to tell. Village in the Shade's farming does far more than the bare minimum. You don't just have basic tilling, but multiple levels to accomodate specific crops; you have composters that can be used to fertilize plots, you have the ability to make paddys to grow rice and other specialized crops. You can craft machines to process materials; to pickle vegetables, smoke meat and eggs, or brew alcohol. You can craft sprinkler systems to help water crops for you; discover magic scarecrows that will let crops from different seasons continue to grow around them. You can upgrade your home and furnish it as you like, Animal Crossing style.
As far as animals go, yes you have your cows and chickens - but you also have ducks, and other more exotic livestock. These even come with their own unique attributes; while you can leave feed growing on your farmland to save time and neglect having to manually feed animals directly every day inside their barn or henhouse, ducks for instance will also feed off of weeds that infest your paddies when left to roam during the day.
Even at a baseline level, Village in the Shade is a great farming sim. I have some small quibbles with the controls - I wish we at least had the option to use the dpad instead of the analog stick, as the game's perspective can make managing vegetables a little less intuitive than it otherwise could have been with a more decisive input method - but even if you ignore my advice and wanted to only pick it up for the Village in the Sunshine mode, the game still gets a hearty recommendation.
What elevates it is everything else, however. That includes hunting with your bow in the mountains - players can purchase hunting licenses to hunt anything from squirrels all the way up to bears - as well as mining and fishing, but what really sets Village in the Shade apart is all of what happens once the sun goes down. In usual farming game fare, once it's dark out you have no choice but to retire to bed; take too long, and you'll usually lose some of your precious daylight in the next day. Things aren't quite so simple here.
A big part of Village in the Shade's story revolves around untangling the meanings for each of Kagatsu Village's rules. The first to be unraveled is the one that states "do not go outside after 11 PM"; the answer is simple, Yokai and all other form of spirits inhabit the village and surrounding areas. Set foot outside after dark, and you'll be given a short interlude to let you know what sort of spirit you're dealing with here. Maybe it will be the Daruma, maybe it will be prowling lanterns; no matter which, they all have their own gimmicks to them, and resources that can be salvages while avoiding their ire.
Find enough cursed items and you can donate them to the shrine outside your farm to gain upgrades; new recipes for crafting, or permanent buffs to things such as your sale price for specific items, or an increase to how quickly you'll build affection with your animals. With each season, players can find a fox that will guide them to an ethereal shrine; donate the requested items - which includes seasonal crops, forageables, and more - and you'll receive the aforementioned magical scarecrows. Complete a shrine's request before the month is up to receive a permanent upgrade to your stamina, which will be essential both for farmwork as well as further exploring the mine.
Fish overnight and you might find a cursed fish; plant mysterious seeds you find for a chance to grow a cursed crop. After unraveling the method, these can be spent to permanently upgrade your health. While most of these overnight excursions revolve around avoiding conflict or finding the one specific trick to drive off spirits - books discovered overnight and which can be donated to the library after it opens include folk stories that offer a hint for how to deal with spirits if you can't discover it on your own - key moments in the story do include boss fights, so it's well worth the effort to seek out these upgrades.
Instead of being two separate experienes, Village in the Shade fully embraces how the things that we keep out of sight do in fact have an impact on our daily lives. This applies to both the story and the gameplay; and it's what transforms it into something truly special. It's almost frustrating how well it's able to swerve from showcasing the beauty of a hand-drawn rural Japanese mountain village, to flipping the script once the lights are out and how unsettling that same locale can be. Combined with what's easily my favorite soundtrack of the year, even with the 70 or so hour runtime.
Do I have my complaints? Of course. While I enjoyed the boss fights, I did think that a few went on just a bit too long. The story, while genuinely incredible once it gets going, does take a while before it starts taking off - and once it does, I concede that it does start getting in the way of the core gameplay. That's part of the point, and I won't say that's a bad thing, but while this is a great farming sim outside of my complaints with the controls (which certainly could eventually be patched, or addressed with a mod on PC) I could see how anyone looking for just a farming sim might find themselves frustrated.
Some of my favorite NIS games have been the result of the team taking a wild swing on something different from their usual fare; Labyrinth of Refrain and Mad Rat Dead come to mind, but I'd be hard-pressed to argue that the team hasn't exceded their prior works with Village in the Shade. It might just be the very best game they've ever released; certainly, it's one of 2026's crowded Fall game releases you won't want to miss..

articles.title_orig: Sutter promised a $1 billion new hospital in the East Bay. Now, it’s pulling the plug
articles.title_zh: Sutter promised a $1 billion new hospital in the East Bay. Now, it’s pulling the plug
articles.content_orig:
Sutter Health has abandoned plans to build a hospital on its Emeryville property, marking a major reversal for the health system’s ambitious proposal to establish a 1.3-million-square-foot medical campus in the city.
In a statement released today , Sutter said it would instead pursue a comprehensive outpatient care campus at its property near Hollis and 53rd streets, while evaluating alternative East Bay locations for a future hospital.
The decision comes after more than a year of planning and regulatory efforts surrounding the proposed hospital, which would have included a 17-story tower with approximately 325 beds, emergency services and a rooftop helipad. The project would have represented one of the largest developments in Emeryville’s history.
Sutter cited uncertainty surrounding the project’s approval process under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) as the primary reason for abandoning the hospital plans. The company said its efforts to secure greater regulatory certainty had failed to protect the project from potential litigation and years of delays.
“The most significant barrier was the lack of a clear and predictable regulatory path,” Sutter Health President and CEO Warner Thomas and Executive Vice President and COO Christina Oh said in the announcement. “Those efforts did not secure the certainty needed to advance the hospital project, leaving it vulnerable to litigation that could delay construction and new hospital services for years.”
Sutter’s revised plans for Emeryville would focus on primary and specialty care, diagnostic services and outpatient surgery. Sutter outlined a range of potential specialties, including women’s and children’s services, heart and digestive care, ENT, urology and orthopedics. Additional services could include imaging, laboratory and pharmacy facilities.
The company said it would continue working with the city through the required approval process, although it has not provided a revised development timeline or details about the size and scope of the outpatient campus.
Sutter said it remains committed to building a new hospital in the East Bay but has not selected an alternative location. The health system is evaluating several potential sites that could accommodate emergency services, advanced clinical care and the infrastructure needed for a modern hospital.
The announcement also leaves the future of Sutter’s Alta Bates Summit Medical Center in Berkeley an important part of the equation. Sutter said there would be no immediate changes to patient care or services at Alta Bates and that it continues to invest in the campus.
The company is also pursuing state legislation that could allow Alta Bates to remain open during the years it would take to plan, approve and construct a replacement hospital. Sutter said it would continue working with state leaders to address regulatory barriers facing hospital construction in California, including consideration of a full CEQA exemption. The company cited the state’s seismic safety requirements and lengthy approval processes as broader challenges to modernizing or replacing aging facilities.
Sutter’s original vision for Emeryville took shape when it acquired the former Emery Yards property from BioMed Realty in early 2025 for approximately $450 million.
The proposal drew significant opposition from nearby residents. Neighbors in Emeryville joined with residents of neighboring Oakland to organize against aspects of the project, forming a citizen group dubbed Emeryville Neighbors United that sought to negotiate a Community Benefits Agreement (CBA) with Sutter. Community concerns were also reflected in the city’s environmental review process, which drew 60 letters from members of the public in response to the Notice of Preparation (NOP) for the Environmental Impact Report. Comments raised concerns about traffic, air quality, noise, pedestrian and bicycle safety, and other potential impacts on surrounding neighborhoods. These and other issues, including potential shadows and wind impacts, were slated for further study as part of the environmental review.
Residents also raised concerns that Sutter’s nonprofit status would exempt the hospital from property taxes, depriving the city of revenue needed to support local services.
The hospital proposal also figured prominently in Emeryville’s upcoming City Council election. Candidate Brandon Soublet made it a prominent theme of his campaign , raising concerns about its potential impacts on surrounding neighborhoods and the city’s ability to manage a development of its scale.
“I’m very glad to see that Sutter listened to the community and developed a right-sized proposal for Emeryville,” Soublet said in response to a request for comment. “If elected, I look forward to working with them to ensure that both Sutter’s and Emeryville residents’ needs are met.”
While Sutter has not disclosed which alternative East Bay locations are under consideration, the company emphasized that Emeryville remains an important part of its regional healthcare strategy.
“Our path has changed, but our commitment has not: expand care in Emeryville, protect hospital access at Alta Bates and create a clear path to the East Bay’s future hospital,” Sutter Health President and CEO Warner Thomas and Executive Vice President and COO Christina Oh wrote in a statement accompanying the announcement.
Sutter said it serves approximately 542,000 patients across the East Bay and will continue providing updates as its plans advance.
Please consider making a recurring contribution at any level you feel comfortable with to help sustain local news for the Emeryville community.
is a third generation Californian and East Bay native who lived in Emeryville from 2003 to 2021. Rob founded The E'ville Eye in 2011 after being robbed at gunpoint and lamenting the lack of local news coverage. Rob's "day job" is as a creative professional .
This is so exciting. I’m excited to see what kind of community benefits we’ll be able to negotiate for their scaled-down and hopefully more realistic new plans for the city.
Oh wow! Amazing to hear that they actually listened to the concerns of the communities and changed their plans! I don’t love that theyre advocating for a CEQA exemption for hospitals… at least that’s not something they can affect quickly.
Jeez. Anything that gives a CEQA exemption spits on us, the citizens.
While I hadn’t studied the situation enough to have an opinion, let me say this article was very informative in bringing me up to speed.
So does this mean that those two vacant piles of dirt are going to remain as vacant piles of dirt? I guess the neighbors got what they wanted..
So now we get a bike lane instead of a 1 billion hospital. You did it bike mafia and NIMBYS.    Hopefully we don’t have a big earthquake any time soon, because Alta Bates will not be fully operational and desperately needs a replacement.
Don’t blame the bike riders. I only ride my bike and the hospital would have been fine. Hortons bike lane would be the same or get better. Hollis was already a mess for bikes.
You are not all bike riders.
I ride a bike too.  But I also drive.
Streets should serve how people want to travel.  Make it too hard for people to drive in East Bay and they’ll just move to Phoenix or Dallas and drive 200 miles a day and blast their AC system, increasing overall carbon emissions.  The east bay is not some isolated closed system utopia.
Congratulations, Emeryville. When Alta Bates closes, you’ll have to head to Summit Hospital in Oakland for your medical care. Unlikely that Sutter will keep that $450 million site just for outpatient care.  Most hospitals build outpatient offices adjacent to a hospital to support the hospital care, and allow doctors easy access to their hospitalized patients, so having offices far away from a hospital makes no sense. They’ll probably sell it and use the money to buy in a community that will welcome them. This is NIMBYism at its finest.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic orders AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games
articles.title_zh: Anthropic orders AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games
articles.content_orig:
Update: Anthropic has confirmed it's released an update to Opus 5.5 to "steer" Claude Code away from "recreating someone else's specific game."
It appears Anthropic may be (quietly) taking action to stem the flood of AI-driven game remakes that have hit the video game industry in the last few month, which saw users creating their own versions of classic and upcoming games, sometimes for fun, sometimes for financial gain.
Earlier today X (formerly Twitter) user Chasm said that they spotted an update to Claude Code's "rules" that was pushed sometime on October 27. The rule is listed under "tengu_heron_brook," and reads "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Do not build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original." Chasm reports that there is no way to disable the rule.
An Anthropic spokesperson referred us to a statement by Anthropic member of technical staff Addy Osmani also posted on X. "We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Osmani wrote. "Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance."
Related: GDC Side Quest - An anti-cheat primer with Lucia Suarez
"In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way."
Fear over the potential of fast-follow AI remakes that might beat the copied game to market has spread among independent developers in the last few weeks. Digital Sun Games is one of several studios to cancel their upcoming public playtest for fear someone might ingest the demo into an AI tool and release their own version of its upcoming game ReVamp . Developers have also pressed Valve to explain how it can prevent the shady clones from supplanting their games on Steam, prompting the company to offer a rare explanation to developers in South Korea earlier in this week .
While developers may take some relief that Anthropic at least doesn't want to actively encourage mass game copying, this rule may only deter the most low-effort copycats. Scientists and reporters have repeatedly documented that safety limits on generative AI tools can be sidestepped by deploying rhetorical tricks . It's also unclear how the software would be able to interpret whether or not a user owns a game idea or game assets.
And as many users responding to Chasm pointed out, if Claude becomes too difficult to use, vibe-coding cloners can turn to open-weight models that have no such restrictions in place.
GameDeveloper.com has reached out to Anthropic for comment and will update this story upon its response.
Related: Epic VP says AI code tools have stomped out decade-old 'non-deterministic cooking bugs' in Unreal Engine
Update 10/30: This story has been updated with confirmation from Anthropic.

His credits include Proxy Studios' 4X strategy game Zephon, Iron Anchor Studios' Down With The Ship, and Amplitude Studio's 2017 game Endless Space 2.

articles.title_orig: Consensus looks elusive at G20 talks after European objections to Russia cancel group photo
articles.title_zh: Consensus looks elusive at G20 talks after European objections to Russia cancel group photo
articles.content_orig:
Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott
The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.
Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.
European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.
During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.
A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.
“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”
The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.
But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

Gold and silver prices tumbled on Friday as rising inflation concerns and expectations of another interest-rate hike weighed on precious metals.
ETFs tracking precious metals fell sharply, with the SPDR Gold Shares (GLD) hitting a fresh 52-week low while the iShares Silver Trust (SLV) slumped to its lowest level in more than 11 months.
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
Spot gold was down 3% to $3,897.17 per ounce, while spot silver dropped more than 6% to $49.08 an ounce, slipping below $50 for the first time since November 2025. Meanwhile, gold futures for December 2026 deliveries declined 3% to $3,910 an ounce.
Analysts have cited the sell-off to inflation concerns from higher energy prices as well as the potential for an interest rate hike later this year.
"Higher oil prices are triggering a risk-off environment, which is triggering a Treasury rally. This is reducing liquidity for equities and gold is getting caught up in the momentum," Bart Melek, global head of commodity strategy at TD Securities, told Bloomberg on Friday.
Peter Grant, vice president and senior ​metals strategist at Zaner Metals, told Reuters that even though major central banks held rates steady this week, the indication was that the "higher-for-longer theme prevails and that's weighing on precious metals."
On Wednesday, the Federal Reserve held rates steady, but traders have increased bets on a rate hike before year-end. According to the CME FedWatch Tool, the odds of a rate hike in December stand at 73%.
Veteran trader Peter Brandt said silver's sharp decline was being driven by investors who bought above $90-$100 per ounce and had previously insisted they would never sell.
He said those investors were now selling their positions and saying they would never buy silver again.
"This is how the start of bottoms are formed," Brandt said in a post on X.
Despite the selloff, retail sentiment surrounding GLD on Stocktwits remained 'bullish' over the past 24 hours. Sentiment turned 'extremely bullish' from 'bullish' for SLV.
SLV is down more than 32% while GLD has declined about 10% so far in 2026.

Anthropic is expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit rating agencies following its initial public offering, according to a report from the Financial Times.
The FT says the investment giant Blackstone, the anchor investor in a recent $63 billion deal to finance Anthropic’s chips, told investors in the deal that it expects the AI lab to receive a “high” junk rating after its IPO. Previously, the FT notes, Blackstone had said the opposite: that the Claude maker would receive an investment-grade rating (indicating low risk for lenders) before 2027 rolls around.
Now Blackstone expects double B range rating, the top tier of speculative “junk” grade, according to the reporting.
TechCrunch reached out to Anthropic and Blackstone but both declined to comment.
Blackstone’s forecast is just a prediction, but naturally, a high junk rating would make it more difficult and costlier for Anthropic to raise the money to keep funding its massive spending that has undergirded its business. The lab has been on a spending spree, racking up large compute power deals throughout the past 12 months, which has worried investors .
Anthropic officially filed to go public earlier this week, kicking off a wave of speculation about how the massive IPO would impact the broader AI industry .

articles.title_orig: As I See It | The flaw in Australia’s ‘China threat’ thesis
articles.title_zh: As I See It | The flaw in Australia’s ‘China threat’ thesis
articles.content_orig:
Instead of adopting Washington’s security priorities, Canberra should leverage superpower rivalry to its own advantage, argues policy veteran John Edwards
Australia’s preparations for a possible conflict with China reflect “a relatively superficial understanding”, argues prominent economist John Edwards. Europe, Canada, Indonesia, Malaysia and India, he notes, are not preparing for such a conflict. Why should Australia?
Instead, he sees US-China rivalry as a potential advantage. Sitting between a security partner in Washington and a major economic partner in Beijing can underpin Australian prosperity for 25 years – provided Canberra does not pick sides.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street abandons ship after gold sinks below $3,900/oz, Main Street maintains bullish majority bias as midterms, payrolls loom
articles.title_zh: Wall Street abandons ship after gold sinks below $3,900/oz, Main Street maintains bullish majority bias as midterms, payrolls loom
articles.content_orig:
Kitco NEWS has a diverse team of journalists reporting on the economy, stock markets, commodities, cryptocurrencies, mining and metals with accuracy and objectivity. Our goal is to help people make informed market decisions through in-depth reporting, daily market roundups, interviews with prominent industry figures, comprehensive coverage (often exclusive) of important industry events and analyses of market-affecting developments.
(Kitco News) – Gold prices suffered another sharp weekly decline, as an early recovery gave way to heavy selling after the Federal Reserve maintained its hawkish stance, stronger U.S. economic data reinforced expectations for further tightening, and Friday's technology-led equity rout triggered widespread liquidation across precious metals.
Spot gold kicked off the week trading at $3,994.95 per ounce on Sunday evening, and the yellow metal initially pushed higher as bargain-hunting emerged following the previous week's selloff below $4,000. The recovery gathered momentum Tuesday as Treasury yields eased and the U.S. dollar softened, carrying gold back above $4,050 ahead of Wednesday's Federal Reserve policy decision. After the Fed voted 10-2 to hold interest rates steady at 3.75% to 4.00%, with two policymakers dissenting in favor of another 25-basis-point hike, spot prices ultimately set their weekly high at $4,082.50 per ounce just before the equity close on Wednesday, before sellers regained control.
Gold came under renewed pressure Thursday after stronger-than-expected third-quarter GDP growth and elevated core PCE inflation reinforced expectations that further monetary tightening could be necessary. The metal slipped back toward $4,000 as the dollar remained supported, despite some relief from easing Treasury yields and lower oil prices.
Selling accelerated dramatically on Friday as a sharp decline in technology stocks, driven by growing concerns over returns on artificial intelligence investment, triggered broader market liquidations. Gold broke decisively below $4,000 and continued falling alongside silver and other precious metals, as forced selling and expectations for another Fed rate hike overwhelmed safe-haven demand. Spot gold ultimately set its weekly low of $3,870.25 per ounce late Friday afternoon – its weakest level in more than a year – and was trading only a few dollars above that level heading into the close.
The latest Kitco News Weekly Gold Survey showed Wall Street bulls abandoning ship after gold sank below $3,900, while Main Street maintained a narrow bullish majority bias despite the yellow metal’s price rout.
“Gold’s shine has dulled,” said Marc Chandler, managing director at Bannockburn Global Forex. “The yellow metal was near $4700 as recently as late August. The one caveat is that the once-more precious metal is below the lower Bollinger Band (two standard deviations below the 20-day moving average. Still, there does not appear to have been a capitulation trade, and assuming a push to new lows for the year, I suspect gold can fall into the $3750-$3850 range.”
“Lower,” said Adam Button, head of currency strategy at investingLive. “It's a big week with the midterms and the potential resumption of the Iran war, but I fear that Trump could lash out and escalate, leading to a severe risk-off trade.”
“I am bearish on Gold for the coming week,” said Colin Cieszynski, chief market strategist at SIA Wealth Management. “Technically, the breakdown below $4,000 is significant.”
“Unchanged,” said Rich Checkan, president and COO of Asset Strategies International. “I see competing influences this coming week. Renewed strikes on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz may bring retaliation soon after U.S. mid-term elections. That should push oil prices higher and stoke inflation concerns… putting downward pressure on gold. But if Democrats make gains in the mid-term elections, it may very well drive uneasy Republicans to the safety and protection of gold.”
“I would treat every drop in gold prices as an opportunity to buy well,” Checkan added.
Daniel Pavilonis, senior commodities broker at StoneX Group, told Kitco News that now that gold and silver have broken near-term critical support, the precious metals may be in for a longer and deeper correction, and gold will need some indication of easing monetary policy to resume the upward trajectory of the last couple of years.
“We're still seeing some inflation,” he said. “We're seeing equities sell off. We're seeing commodities have come off, except for some of the energy sector.
Pavilonis said the market is in the midst of an unwind. “If you're looking at the charts, they don't look so hot... If you're just looking at this from a technical standpoint, not any fundamentals, it looks like we could go lower.”
As for how low the precious metals could slide, Pavilonis said the metals could be in for a deep pullback before sustained buying resumes.
“I could see silver getting as low as the high $30s,” he said. “I could see gold getting as low as somewhere around $3,000. I think it's very likely to happen into the first quarter of next year, and then maybe just base out for a little while, and then possibly move higher.”
Pavilonis said he’s seen this time and time again. “What happened the last few times when silver hit $50, when gold spikes up? We sell off afterward,” he said. “The party is over. The themes that we [saw at the early 2026 highs], the same headlines, the same stories… because of inflation, because of this or that. People need to rationalize why it went up so much. But if you go back into the archives and look at news around 1980 – before people realized it was the Hunt brothers, which was part of the story – but it was the same thing: ‘We're running out of silver, we're running out of gold, the exchanges are low, warehouses are low, inventories… And people are buying, and so you’ve got to go out and buy some gold, go out and buy some silver!’ There were almost identical New York Times articles being written about silver and gold in the run-up to 1980.”
“Now I think that anybody from the move to the upside that hasn't been stopped out, or is holding on the physical side, It's time to hedge,” he said. “You want to start collaring around positions. You want to start collaring and capitalizing on it. Because if it does go lower, then there's ways to mitigate that, put yourself in the right position where you can accumulate more. That's what I would be thinking about right now.”
Pavilonis said that if we see further liquidations across financial markets, he expects to see more selling of gold as well.
“We have this rationale to buy and hold onto the metals,” he said. “I think in the long term you're going to be right. But in the short term, the thesis can be wrong, so it's time to maybe even hedge a little bit further if you haven't already.”
This week, 16 analysts participated in the Kitco News Gold Survey, with Wall Street’s bullish belief all but evaporating after gold couldn’t hold $3,900. Only one expert, or 6%, expected to see gold prices gain ground during the week ahead, while 10, representing 63%, saw the yellow metal declining further. The remaining five analysts, 31% of the total, said they couldn’t predict gold’s direction, or expected sideways trading next week.
Meanwhile, 184 votes were cast in Kitco’s online poll, with Main Street investors once again more bullish than their professional counterparts despite gold’s steep selloff. 98 retail traders, or 53%, looked for gold prices to rise next week, while 56 others, or 30%, predicted the yellow metal would lose further ground. The remaining 30 investors, representing 16% of the total, expected to see price consolidation during the week ahead.
Next week will feature top-tier economic data and geopolitical risk events for investors to navigate, with the U.S. midterm elections and October’s nonfarm payrolls report the most significant of a raft of market-movers.

The U.S. Department of Defense has added two more service member deaths to its official account of casualties since the war with Iran started more than eight months ago, bringing the overall death toll to 23.
Both of the newly noted deaths on the Defense Casualty Analysis System portal were noncombat related. In total the DCAS portal says 11 service members have been killed by enemy fire during the war, and 12 others have died under circumstances deemed nonhostile, which includes accidents and sickness.
Both of the service members recently added as nonhostile deaths were airmen, including one who died of an illness and the another from unspecified causes that remain under investigation, The Washington Post quoted the Air Force as saying.
The two deaths added to the DCAS system are listed under Overseas Operations , which includes deaths recorded by the Pentagon after it stopped using the name Operation Epic Fury for the offensive against Iran in May, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared the operation over.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Friday it intercepted and destroyed a drone in the Mecca region that had been fired by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels.
"A drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Mecca region," the coalition wrote in a post on X.
The Houthis denied any attempt to strike Saudi Arabia on Friday, the Reuters news agency reports.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on social media that the group hadn't conducted any operations aimed at Saudi territory, adding that the Houthis only target Saudi oil facilities and military bases.
Explosions rocked the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh on Thursday hours after the Iran-backed Houthis reported deadly strikes earlier in the day on residential areas of western Yemen that the Houthis said killed at least 12 people.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said on Thursday it had downed two ballistic missiles launched by the group towards Riyadh, soon after Agence France-Presse correspondents heard fresh explosions in the capital.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said on X.
Earlier, AFP correspondents in Riyadh had heard at least eight explosions as authorities warned the city was "under a hostile aerial threat" in a phone alert.
Saudi civil defense had issued warnings for "potential danger" in Riyadh, Kharj and the southern city of Najran that were lifted shortly afterward.
The Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including by launching deadly strikes on the Riyadh airport that forced its shuttering for two weeks as flagship events were canceled, threatening the kingdom's economic diversification plans.
The Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government have exchanged daily attacks since a yearslong truce fell apart over the summer.
A tanker was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz around 7:30 p.m. local time (noon Eastern time), according to the U.K. Marine Trade Operations Centre .
The ship was exiting the strait along the southern route, promoted by the U.S., when it came under fire.
"There are no reported injuries to the crew or environmental impact … at this time," the UKMTO said.
While it wasn't clear who fired the projectile, Iran has taken credit for several ships hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday and has been targeting ships along the southern route at an increased rate.
Iran has not yet responded to a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance to the secretary of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, according to the semi-official Tasnim News agency, which is closely affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Tasnim said in a Thursday post on its official Telegram social media account that Tehran was not prepared to drop any of its core conditions for a ceasefire, which include lifting the American blockade of Iran's ports, easing sanctions and giving Iran access to its frozen financial assets held abroad, among other things.
Multiple news outlets have reported that Vance's letter to Rezaei was an attempt to restart peace negotiations, but President Trump said Wednesday that it was a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Iran's navy said a tanker it described as violating maritime restrictions was damaged and caught fire after striking sea mines east of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the vessel unable to continue sailing.
In a statement, the navy said the incident occurred before noon on Thursday as the tanker was sailing through an area designated as prohibited and unsafe by Iran
The U.S. has encouraged shippers to use a shipping route in the south of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has insisted vessels can only use northern routes it has authorized.
The navy's statement warned that the Strait of Hormuz was closed "to violating vessels that, without coordination and relying on the lies of the U.S. president, intend to pass through prohibited and unsafe areas."
"These uncoordinated transits through high-risk areas have exposed and will continue to expose vessels and their crews to serious dangers," it added.
Qatar has categorically denied allegations of interfering in Israel's elections or funding efforts to influence their outcome, accusing Israeli politicians and media figures of launching a disinformation campaign to drag the small Persian Gulf state into domestic Israeli political disputes.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Majid al-Ansari said in a statement that Qatar would not be used as a scapegoat for Israeli politicians' failures, insisting that Doha had no involvement in Israel's political competition and would continue its mediation efforts between Iran and the U.S., as well as wider diplomatic engagement and support for the Palestinian people.
His comments come after Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu alleged that Tuesday's national elections were "stolen by Arab parties" and claimed foreign interference in the vote.
Israel's Shin Bet internal security service is investigating possible Qatari and Turkish funding used in an effort to influence the election outcome, according to reports by the Jerusalem Post and Israel's Channel 13.
"These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure," al-Ansari said. "The repeated invocation of Qatar in Israeli electoral rhetoric reveals an excessive obsession with our country among certain Israeli political and media figures."
Iran's navy has carried out more than 20 operations against U.S. warships and approximately 300 operations targeting American interests in various locations during the war, Iranian Army Navy Coordinating Deputy Rear Admiral Jalil Moghadam said in an interview published Thursday by the official state-run news agency IRNA .
Moghadam claimed the operations involved missiles and drones and said Iran's navy remains operational despite repeated claims by President Trump and other U.S. officials saying it has been destroyed.
"If the Iranian Navy has been destroyed, why have these forces not come closer than 500 or 600 kilometers to the Strait of Hormuz, or closer than 300 kilometers to our maritime borders? There is a force standing in their way, and that force must be the Navy," he said.

articles.title_orig: China’s Fourth Aircraft Carrier Could Arrive as Soon as Next Year
articles.title_zh: China’s Fourth Aircraft Carrier Could Arrive as Soon as Next Year
articles.content_orig:
By ELINA SHIRAZI, US SENIOR POLITICAL REPORTER
Published: 13:43 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 18:12 EDT, 30 October 2026
A dramatic surge in military tension has taken center stage as President Trump ordered a third US aircraft carrier to the Middle East – all while making cryptic claims that the standoff will soon reach its conclusion.
US Central Command confirmed that bringing three aircraft carrier strike groups into the Middle East represents the largest US naval surge in the region since the 2003 invasion of Iraq .
Trump voiced confidence today that the conflict would dissipate, though he provided no specific timeline or strategy for how that outcome would be secured.
'It's going to get wrapped up soon,' Trump stated during an interview with a Kansas City radio station. 'We need a guarantee there'll never be a nuclear weapon.'
The remarks comes as questions surrounding Trump's domestic campaign itinerary arise, with the President rescheduling several canceled rallies over the weekend.
Vice President JD Vance also canceled a scheduled Friday press briefing in St. Cloud, Minnesota , focused on the administration's 'War on Fraud.'
Officials have not provided a reason for the cancellation.
Recent reports suggest the administration is laying the groundwork for a fresh wave of aggressive military strikes if Iranian leaders refuse to sign an agreement.
The aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln is pictured
During campaign appearances, he has argued that hostilities will wrap up shortly following the midterms, provided the GOP retains control of Congress
Despite initiating the war in February expecting a rapid surrender from Iran's weakened regime, Trump has continuously maintained that the conflict will draw to a close, even while combat intensifies and global economic damage continues to mount.
This has led to voter dissatisfaction across both parties ahead of the midterm elections.
During campaign appearances, he has argued that hostilities will wrap up shortly following the midterms, provided the GOP retains control of Congress.
Two US officials report that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit are scheduled to arrive in the Middle East by late November.
Upon arrival, the Roosevelt will operate alongside the USS George H.W. Bush, which deployed in April, and the USS George Washington, which arrived in August as a replacement for the USS Abraham Lincoln.
Meanwhile, the nation's highest–ranking Middle East commander has reportedly briefed Trump on potential strike scenarios regarding Iran.
Admiral Brad Cooper visited the White House on Thursday with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and General Dan Caine, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Wall Street Journal reports.
As Trump evaluates strategy options for resuming military action against Iran, the discussion with cabinet officials included potential plans for maintaining the ongoing regional blockade.
Following a high-level White House meeting involving military leadership and Vice President Vance, Hegseth removed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia from his role as top strategist for the Joint Chiefs.
Sylvia's removal comes amid allegations that he leaked classified intelligence regarding the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: Chaos at Poland's constitutional court as government-backed judges seek to oust chief justice
articles.title_zh: Chaos at Poland's constitutional court as government-backed judges seek to oust chief justice
articles.content_orig:
Riot police have been deployed at Poland's Constitutional Court amid an escalating stand-off between the government and the court's top judges.
The row pits the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk against his predecessors from the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS).
The police intervention came after Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said he had requested stripping the court's President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański of their immunity from prosecution to bring criminal charges against them.
Tusk has vowed to depoliticise the judiciary, and on Friday defended the move as PiS supporters gathered outside the court premises in Warsaw in protest.
President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, has now entered the constitutional court, according to his chief of staff.
Nawrocki cancelled a trip to Senegal mid-air in order to attend to the confrontation in Warsaw. He had been on his way to the Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar.
Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.
In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.
"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.
In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."
The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.
Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.
The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.
Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.
Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Court judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.
One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.
Earlier this month, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, the Venice Commission, said Nawrocki should swear-in the judges to allow them to sit on the court's bench.
Justice Minister Żurek said Święczkowski and his vice-president should face criminal charges for not allowing the judges to adjudicate.
Some of Tusk's supporters have accused him of failing to act decisively to reverse the PiS-era reforms.
Parliamentary elections are scheduled next year, and some see his move as an attempt to boost Tusk's popularity among those voters.
But his actions have been criticised. In September, Tusk put forward a politician, Maciej Berek, a lawyer who served as a minister in his cabinet, as a judge candidate to the court.
Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski  to be the court's worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis "for a million reasons".
"Today's action at the Constitutional Court, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades," Prof Matczak wrote on social media.
"Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Court by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come," he added.

articles.title_orig: Mass protests sweep Italy during nationwide strike
articles.title_zh: Mass protests sweep Italy during nationwide strike
articles.content_orig:
ROME — Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.
The demonstrations were largely peaceful but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protestors and groups of police charging to disperse protestors in Rome on Friday night.
After several weeks of violent protests in Italy and throughout Europe , more widespread disruption is expected after the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) and other trade unions called on workers in both the public and private sectors to strike and protest.
The demonstrations in Italy appear to have been partly inspired by those in France , where some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider actions about the cost of living and social security.
Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.
In Rome, many waved communist and Palestinian flags, as well as signs against the Iran war. Some let off pink smoke bombs. There was a jovial mood among the demonstrators as they lined up before the march, as has often been the case early on at previous protests, only for violence to break out later.
Protesters storm the Colosseum in Rome
Giovanna Di Matteo, a member of the left-wing Potere al Popolo! party, said she was protesting against the government that “did nothing for the people of this country.”
The government had spent money on the military “while they cut on welfare, they cut on services and people cannot reach the end of the month,” she said. “They have no money for their houses, they have no money for gasoline and everything.”
Luca, a 20-year-old medical student said the protesters felt they were “still not being heard, that everything is still the same,” and the government didn’t “care about our voice, about our voices, and about the future of this nation that is our nation.”
“We have been completely screwed by the fact that the wages do not keep up on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the cost of living,” added Luca, who asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.
Major demonstrations also took place in other cities and towns across Italy.
They came after a number of protests in recent weeks have turned violent. Groups of masked protesters looted stores in Milan and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons earlier this month.
Italian police were out in force again Friday with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the Rome protest.
Their presence was heavy after protesters stormed Rome’s historic Colosseum on Saturday, while in the south, farmers and truckers have blockaded highways and ports to protest high fuel prices which have risen since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni , who has made law and order a key tenet of her administration, said she had “great respect” for peaceful protesters on X earlier this month.
But her right-wing government has since introduced tougher penalties for rioters, including financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalizing and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media after unveiling the legislation.
The government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year.
NBC News Chief Foreign Correspondent
Sara Monetta is a multimedia producer based in London.

articles.title_zh: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
articles.content_orig:
As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.﻿
As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.﻿
Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. During his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he also commented on AI’s impact on math , Altman said:
“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.
But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”
Whether Altman meant your gaming PC or developers working with something like the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box or the new touchscreen MacBook Pro , the outcome is the same. Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years. And the billions they’re willing to lay out for chips is why the laptops, phones, and other tech you use are getting more expensive right now.

articles.title_orig: G20 drops group photo as Europeans refuse to stand with Lavrov
articles.title_zh: G20 drops group photo as Europeans refuse to stand with Lavrov
articles.content_orig:
The United States has scrapped a traditional group photo of foreign ministers after European officials refused to be pictured alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
The move exposes deep rifts at the heart of the Group of 20 (G20), whose foreign ministers are meeting in the southern city of Atlanta in the United States for talks overshadowed by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
“There will be no family photo featuring our European partners together with Mr Lavrov,” German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said, according to the dpa news agency.
Lavrov, who remains under Western sanctions imposed after Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, arrived in Atlanta ahead of the talks, Russian state media reported. Moscow said on Thursday that he would use his speech to argue against international sanctions. Ukraine was not invited, the Abu Dhabi-based newspaper The National reported.
A diplomatic source told the AFP news agency that Russia’s presence at the G20 “in no way legitimises its actions”.
The European Union’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas pledged on Thursday to urge G20 partners to strengthen support for Ukraine and pursue accountability through a special tribunal and claims commission, after a Russian strike on a Ukrainian railway station killed at least 14 people earlier that day.
The meeting also comes weeks after US President Donald Trump issued sanctions waivers allowing Russia to export diesel to ease fuel prices before the November 3 midterm elections.
Opening the talks, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged members to cooperate on economic and geopolitical crises threatening global trade, energy and food supplies, and freedom of navigation, dpa reported. Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz after US-Israeli strikes began in late February, and global energy prices have risen sharply since.
“Both maritime and food security drive economic security,” Rubio wrote on X.
No joint statement is expected. A diplomatic source told the AFP news agency that Washington will instead publish a chair’s summary it has drafted. The source added: “The G20 is no longer really a forum where foreign ministers can reach agreement on a statement.”
No government has said whether Rubio and Lavrov will hold a formal bilateral meeting.
China sent Executive Vice Foreign Minister Ma Zhaoxu in place of Foreign Minister Wang Yi, according to a delegation list released by the Department of State. South Africa, a founding G20 member, has been excluded by Washington, and the African Union is represented by Burundi’s Edouard Bizimana.
The Atlanta talks are the last ministerial meeting of the US G20 presidency before leaders meet in Miami on December 14 and 15.

Polish president Karol Nawrocki turned back his plane en route to Senegal on Friday as the country’s top court was thrown into chaos after its president was suspended.
Police and protesters clashed outside the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw after the government suspended its two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges against them. Reports suggest riot police were deployed on Friday evening as demonstrators supporting the Law and Order (PiS) party, who oppose the government, threw objects at officers.
"At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland . I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning," Mr Nawrocki, who is backed by the PiS, said on X.
The tribunal ⁠said on its website that the court's president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, ​had ⁠been suspended on Friday.
A ‌long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution.
Earlier this year, Mr Nawrocki, an ally of ‌Poland's former nationalist government of the Law ‌and Justice or PiS party, refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, who was a deputy ⁠justice minister under PiS, declined to allow judges elected by the current parliamentary majority to assume their duties.
Restoring the rule of law is the government's duty, prime minister Donald Tusk said on X later on Friday.
“Restoring the rule of law is our obligation,” prime minister Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening. “After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.”
Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek told ‌reporters he has requested the ⁠lifting of the immunities of Swieczkowski and his deputy ⁠for failing to fulfill their duties by preventing judges from performing their ‌work.
PiS politicians, ​including leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski, said Tusk's ‌government was carrying out a ​coup on the tribunal.
